query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Parts made from a tungsten‐based refractory high-entropy alloy incorporating controlled coherent nanoprecipitates will exhibit significantly improved resistance to erosion by high-temperature liquid aluminum compared to conventional materials used in hot dip aluminum plating equipment.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-fabricated tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy with a microstructure engineered to contain coherent nanoprecipitates.
generation.intervention: Fabricate critical dipping and plating equipment parts (e.g., rollers and guide plates) from the tungsten-based refractory HEA.
generation.conditions: Long-term exposure to molten aluminum at temperatures encountered in hot dip plating operations.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence of coherent nanoprecipitates within the tungsten-rich matrix that stabilize the microstructure and promote formation of a protective, adherent oxide scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The high melting point and intrinsic corrosion resistance of the tungsten-based HEA, in combination with the engineered nanoprecipitates that facilitate stress relief and aid in forming a stable protective oxide layer, reduce direct chemical attack by molten aluminum.
generation.predicted_outcome: Equipment parts made from this HEA will show lower rates of material loss (erosion), maintain superior mechanical integrity, and thus provide a longer service life than parts made from conventional alloys under similar hot dip processing conditions.
generation.baseline: Parts currently made from conventional alloys that undergo significant erosion and require frequent maintenance or replacement due to prolonged contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.boundary: This protective effect is expected to be valid under the typical temperature and chemical conditions of hot dip aluminum plating; performance under extreme thermal cycling or in the presence of unexpected impurities may vary.
generation.uncertainty: While the high-temperature strength and oxidation resistance of tungsten-based refractory HEAs are promising, the exact quantitative improvement in erosion resistance and the long-term stability of the protective oxide scale in a real plating environment remain to be experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of dipping equipment parts: one set using the tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy with engineered coherent nanoprecipitates, and a control set using the current conventional alloy. Operate both sets under identical hot dip aluminum plating conditions for a prolonged period, including planned thermal cycling that mimics industrial processing.
measurements: Quantitative mass loss/erosion rates measured periodically
Surface analysis (e.g., XRD, SEM/EDS) to assess protective oxide scale formation and integrity
Mechanical property tests before and after exposure (e.g., tensile or hardness measurements)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, EBSD) to verify stability of nanoprecipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-based HEA parts do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in erosion (mass loss), do not maintain a robust protective oxide layer, or if no meaningful extension in service life is observed relative to the control parts under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date.
